You are skeptic #2. A WCAG/§4 audit of Heard's "provider-sessions" screen produced this finding. Independently verify it by READING the cited code. Try to REFUTE it — default to real=false if the code already handles it, the claim is a stylistic nit, or it's not actually reachable by a user.

FILE: /Users/taha/Claude projects/TEWW apps/Therapy (Heard)/app/(provider)/provider/sessions/page.tsx
LOCATION: Lines 48–50
RULE: 4
TITLE: Invalid nested interactive elements (Link > Button)
DETAIL: The Link element wraps a Button element. This creates nested `<a><button>` which is semantically invalid and breaks keyboard navigation and screen reader interpretation. When a user presses Enter on the link, only the link activates; the button is unreachable by tab order and may be skipped by assistive technology.
SUGGESTION: Replace the Link/Button pattern with either: (1) an `<a href>` that looks like a button (safest); or (2) make the entire Card clickable via a parent link. Example: `<Link href={...} className='...'><Card as='li'>{content}</Card></Link>` or keep the interactive element singular.

Return real=true ONLY if this is a genuine, actionable accessibility/polish gap that a fix would meaningfully improve.

input.reason: The code renders <a><button> nesting (Link > Button), which is semantically confusing and violates accessibility best practices. While HTML5 technically allows nested interactive elements and the pattern functionally works (the link navigates), it creates redundant interactive semantics that confuse screen readers, wastes keyboard focus stops, and violates WCAG design principles. The suggestion to use a single interactive element (either <a> styled as a button or a simple link wrapper) would meaningfully improve semantic clarity and keyboard/AT user experience. This is a genuine actionable gap, not a stylistic nit.
